title: The Death of the Professional-Managerial Class
author: John B. Judis
content:
![The Death of the Professional-Managerial
Class](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/Screenshot_2025-08-10_at_12.10.39
---PM-1.jpg)

In the wake of Kamala Harris's defeat in 2024, one heard often that Democrats
needed to focus on class rather than identity. But what exactly does it mean
to focus on class? And what class is it that Democrats need to focus on? The
party's surging left wing has a clear answer--the working class--and usually
offers an expansive conception of who is included in that category. "I think
if you have to work to pay your bills," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has
[_said_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/18/magazine/zohran-mamdani-
interview.html?ref=compactmag.com), "I think that is one definition of being a
part of the working class."

However, some have taken exception to this characterization and questioned
whether Democrats like Mamdani are really speaking to the working class.
Citing the high levels of education and relative affluence of voters
supporting progressive candidates, they claim that Mamdani and his allies'
true base is the "professional-managerial class," or PMC.

As one writer recently put it, "The 'PMC,' as it has become known, was
beginning to dominate the political left even in 1977; today, it arguably
forms the Democratic Party's most important voter base." In the words of
another, "Fifty years ago, the professional-managerial class swung right.
Today, in America's biggest cities, they're voting for leftists like Zohran
Mamdani."

The idea of the PMC was
[_popularized_](https://libcom.org/article/professional-managerial-class-
barbara-and-john-ehrenreich?ref=compactmag.com) by the left-wing social
critics John and Barbara Ehrenreich in a 1976 essay in _Radical America_. Over
the past decade, writers from various points on the political spectrum have
revived versions of this concept in discussions of resurgent progressive
politics, from [_Julius
Krein_](https://americanaffairsjournal.org/2019/11/the-real-class-
war/?ref=compactmag.com) and [_Michael
Lind_](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/607661/the-new-class-war-by-
michael-lind/?ref=compactmag.com) to [_Gabriel
Winant_](https://www.nplusonemag.com/online-only/online-only/professional-
managerial-chasm/?ref=compactmag.com) and Catherine Liu, whose 2021
[_book_](https://www.upress.umn.edu/9781517912253/virtue-
hoarders/?ref=compactmag.com) was entitled _Virtue Hoarders: The Case against
the Professional-Managerial Class_.

Is the distinction between the working class and the professional-managerial
class, common to all these accounts, useful? Returning to the origins of the
PMC concept makes clear how it seemed plausible at the time, but also why it
has now outlived its usefulness except as a polemical term against left-wing
politicians.

Before the Ehrenreichs wrote their _Radical America_ essay, they had
introduced the idea of the professional-managerial class in debates within the
New American Movement (NAM), a socialist organization to which they and I
belonged. (NAM later merged with Michael Harrington's Democratic Socialist
Organizing Committee to form the Democratic Socialists of America.) The
Ehrenreichs had several targets in mind when they formulated the idea of the
PMC, but the principal one was the idea of a diversified working class that
several of us at the journal _Socialist Revolution_ had developed, which had
become inscribed in the New American Movement's political platform.

The starting point of these debates was Karl Marx's conception of class
struggle as the fulcrum of political transformation. Marx defined membership
in a class by a person's relationship to the process of production. Owners
were capitalists; workers who had to sell their labor power to capitalists
were members of the working class. One's consciousness of being either a
worker or owner is or can be integral to a collective politics. This common
consciousness does not need to be articulated in the words "working class." An
agitator might instead use terms like "working people" or simply "the people."
But the shared position of workers was the basis for a common struggle against
owners.

Some Marxist theorists have relied on the historian E.P. Thompson's argument
that English industrial workers didn't become a class until they were
conscious of being one. Class consciousness, for Thompson, is something that
is "made" in the course of a class struggle and is premised on the awareness
of a common condition and common adversary. In the United States in 1976 and
today, there is not a "working class" unified in its understanding of itself.
The question, then, is what might prove the basis for the emergence of such an
understanding.

> "Marx's dynamic conception of class and of the class struggle has endured."

Marx's theory was that as capitalism suffered persistent and growing crises,
workers would organize themselves into unions, form a party, become conscious
of their common condition, and attempt to wrest control of the government and
economy from the capitalist class. Theses suppositions proved wanting, but
Marx's dynamic conception of class and of the class struggle has endured, and
is taken for granted in controversy over the professional-managerial class and
the working class. For all participating in the debate, class defines a common
condition that is conducive to a collective struggle.

* * *

Marxists have debated why Marx's predictions hadn't come to pass since the
late nineteenth century, but the rise of the New Left in the 1960s posed a
challenge to the specifics of Marx's theory of class. The New Left began as a
liberal reform movement to secure racial justice and to demand a negotiated
peace in Vietnam, but by the middle of the decade, it acquired a radical edge,
with many of its militants arguing that the only way to end racial injustice
and imperial wars was through a revolution. New Left groups called themselves
"socialist" or even "communist" even though their core constituency wasn't
industrial laborers but college students and recent graduates. (The Students
for a Democratic Society, or SDS, is an obvious case, but even the Black
Panther Party was founded by two students at Merritt College in Oakland.)

Some of these socialist political tendencies, typified by the group
Progressive Labor, fell back on the traditional Marxist idea of class
struggle. Holding fast to the orthodox Marxist view that only blue-collar
workers could bring about revolutionary change, they sent their members to
work in factories, as truck drivers, or in related occupations. Other groups,
typified by the Black Panther Party and the radical SDS splinter group
Weatherman, abandoned any notion of the working class as the revolutionary
subject. They argued instead that blacks, and sometimes other minorities, were
part of a global anti-imperialist movement against American power.
Organizations dominated by whites could function as auxiliaries to Third World
revolutionaries. By their account, blacks in the US were colonized subjects,
and their struggle was an anti-colonial one.

Those of us who joined the New American Movement, founded in 1971, saw
ourselves as the descendants of the original SDS, which had promoted
participatory democracy and shunned Marxist-Leninist orthodoxy. But the New
American Movement was also an attempt to reconcile the older Marxist theory of
class with the development of service workers and professionals who now
outnumbered blue-collar factory workers. The explosion of college attendance
after World War II, and particularly in the '60s, had swelled the ranks of
college-graduates who worked for wages and salaries and were under the
authority of managers and executives. The New American Movement saw these new
workers, its _Political Perspective_ of June 1972 declared, as part of
"increasingly diversified and stratified working class created by large-scale
corporate capitalism." The document, which the late James Weinstein and I had
a hand in writing, went on to state: "The task of socialists is to clarify the
origins of the internal divisions in the working class and to find the basis
for unity."

> "We were trying to describe an incipient majority that could win power."

Our idea of a diversified proletariat did not describe an existing class
consciousness, but the basis for developing one, whether it explicitly went by
the name of "working class" or not. It was meant to describe an incipient
majority that could win power. It was based structurally on opposition to a
capitalist class, which even if it didn't directly employ a nurse or a
janitor, did so indirectly through the power it wielded over the state and its
expenditures. There were, to be sure, differences in income and social
standing between the parts of this diversified proletariat, but the key to a
common understanding was that the college-educated were increasingly subject
to what Marxists called proletarianization.

Like the craft workers of the nineteenth century who found themselves robbed
of their status and autonomy and deskilled by the industrialization of their
professions, the college-educated white-collar workers were increasingly
subject to a loss of autonomy. That was particularly significant for the so-
called professionals who judged their products primarily by standards of
excellence rather than profitability. Teachers were judged by whether their
pupils learned; nurses and doctors by how well they treated their patients;
software developers by whether they produced "cool code." (During this period,
I published an interview in _Socialist Revolution_ with a computer programmer
who in those days was still using punch cards.)

Marx had depicted the working class as a "universal class" whose interests
were identical with those of the society as a whole. For Marx and for the
early socialists, that meant the working class was equipped to govern society.
In _The Promise of American Life_ , which appeared in 1909, the progressive
journalist Herbert Croly ridiculed that idea. "The action of a majority
composed of the ordinary type of convinced socialists," he wrote, "could and
would in a few years do more to make socialism impossible than could be
accomplished by the best and most prolonged efforts of a majority of malignant
anti-socialists." Croly's quip was not entirely unwarranted. However, a decade
later, Thorstein Veblen prophesied in _Engineers and the Price System_ that
the widespread employment of engineers and technicians would raise the
possibility of self-government without a capitalist class. NAM's concept of a
diversified working class incorporated Veblen's optimism about self-
government. This new working class, we argued, was equipped with the skills to
manage an economy and govern a country.

Inside the New American Movement, the debate with the Ehrenreichs over the
nature of the working class began in the mid-1970s and came to a head with
their essay in _Radical America_ , which drew a sharp distinction between the
working class and the professional-managerial class. The working class
consisted of "craftsmen, operatives, laborers, sales workers, clerical
workers, service workers, [and] non-college educated technical workers." The
shorthand Marxist version would be wage-laborers engaged in the production and
distribution of commodities, but it might extend to include lower-level office
workers in finance, whom Marx would have regarded as unproductive workers.

For its part, the professional-managerial class included not only nurses,
welfare workers, teachers, entertainers, writers, engineers and other
technical workers, but also "middle-level administrators and managers." The
Ehrenreichs defined the PMC as "salaried mental workers who do not own the
means of production and whose major function in the social division of labor
may be described broadly as the reproduction of capitalist culture and class
relations." Schoolteachers and entertainers, for instance, are "directly
concerned with social control or with the production and propagation of
ideology."

On this basis, the Ehrenreichs stipulated that members of the PMC were
"objectively antagonistic" to the working class--that is, they were a distinct
class with opposing interests that couldn't be grouped together, as the
proponents of a diversified working class had suggested, in a coalition
against the ruling class of business and financial magnates. This point would
seem obvious in the case of middle managers and administrators, who could be
expected to side with their immediate superiors. But the Ehrenreichs also held
that registered nurses, schoolteachers, or actors occupied an objectively
antagonistic stance toward factory workers, truck drivers, and grocery
cashiers.

Their argument derived in part from a visit to China in 1975. The Ehrenreichs,
as I learned when they stayed at our house in Oakland after their return, had
come to admire the Chinese Cultural Revolution. "Our exposure to the tail end
of the Cultural Revolution in China and our involvement in the developing
feminist critique of professionalism here fed into our thinking about the
class dynamics of the American left," they
[_wrote_](https://a.co/d/0g0Hcobq?ref=compactmag.com) in reply to critics of
their thesis. They were particularly taken by the Chinese attempt to remove
the "conflict between manual and mental workers" by forcing mental workers to
integrate with and share the labors of manual workers. That effort, they
believed, was preventing the deskilling of the working class that had taken
place earlier in the United States.

A feminist critique of expertise was another key influence on the Ehrenreichs'
thinking. In the United States, beginning in the late nineteenth century,
activities like medical care and education had been transferred from working
class communities to experts hired by cities, states, and the federal
government. The PMC, they wrote, existed "by virtue of expropriation of the
skills and culture once indigenous to the working class." They went on to
state: "The professional-manager workers exist. only by virtue of the
expropriation of the skills and culture once indigenous to the working class."
Feminists had made this argument about midwives and obstetricians, but the
Ehrenreichs extended to the working class as a whole.

In the mid-1970s, the Ehrenreichs had on their side the fact that many
professionals, whose autonomy and income was protected by guild-like
professional associations, and who often owned their own firms or worked in
partnerships in small firms, did think politically like middle managers. They
were likely to be free-market Republicans, and large numbers of them backed
Ronald Reagan in the 1980 and 1984 elections. According to the American
National Election Studies (ANES) surveys, a majority of professionals did not
back a Democratic presidential candidate until 1988. But after that, the basis
for grouping professionals together with managers weakened--and with it, the
basis for the Ehrenreichs' account of the PMC.

* * *

Since the 1980s, if not earlier, professionals and managers have diverged in
their party and candidate choices; professionals have increasingly backed
Democrats, while managers have stuck with the Republicans. In his 2010
[_book_](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691143934/red-state-
blue-state-rich-state-poor-state?ref=compactmag.com), _Red State Blue State_ ,
political scientist Andrew Gelman, using American National Election Studies
data, charted the different presidential choices of occupational groups:

![The Death of the Professional-Managerial
Class](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/data-
src-image-5d6a1c75-feb0-4832-a320-3a4e7eae2418.png)

The downward trajectory shows professionals moving away from Republicans, even
as support of Republicans remained consistent among managers.

One could argue that an occupational group's choice of party candidate has no
bearing on its class consciousness. But on at least one defining class issue,
Democrats are 45 percentage points more likely to approve of labor unions than
Republicans, according to Gallup. Likewise back-of-the-envelope tabulation
based on the 2024 General Social Survey shows that while there is no
significant
[_difference_](https://gssdataexplorer.norc.org/analysis_summary/89271?creatorId=106269&back=tabulation&ref=compactmag.com)
in the responses of managers and professionals when it comes to, say,
abortion, 80 percent of professionals reported
[_having_](https://gssdataexplorer.norc.org/analysis_summary/89271?creatorId=106269&back=tabulation%20%20confiden%20in%20labo&ref=compactmag.com)
at least some confidence in labor unions, while a majority of managers
reported having "hardly any."

Moreover, managers are not organized into unions--if anything, they are the
antagonists of unions--while professionals now account for many of the members
of the four largest labor unions: the National Education Association, the
Service Employees International Union, the American Federation of Teachers,
and the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees. Among
the professionals represented by SEIU are doctors, registered nurses,
physician assistants, pharmacists, physical therapists, social workers,
research technicians, lawyers, engineers, court employees, librarians, IT
professionals, law enforcement officers, adjunct professors, university
researchers, academic counselors, and K-12 early learning professionals.

I could find no comprehensive studies of the political differences between
American professionals and managers, but University of Toronto sociologist
D.W. Livingstone has written on how Canadian professionals differ in class
outlook from managers. In [__Tipping Point for Advanced
Capitalism__](https://fernwoodpublishing.ca/books/tipping-point-for-advanced-
capitalism?ref=compactmag.com), Livingstone analyzed surveys of workers in
Canada, the United States, and Western Europe to see how they would respond to
questions of whether owners of corporations should be able to make gains at
the expense of their workers and whether corporations should be prohibited
from replacing striking workers. He found a sharp difference between
professional employees and managers on two of these questions: "whether owners
of corporations make gains at the expense of their workers" and where
"management should be prohibited by law from hiring workers to take the place
of strikers." Livingstone _rated_ the responses as either pro-labor, pro-
capital, or contradictory. Professionals' answers, he found, were most similar
to those of industrial workers and diverged from those of corporate
capitalists, large employers and upper managers.

 _Class by Oppositional Class Consciousness, Canada, 1982-2016_  
(%pro-labor/pro-capital views / contradictory views excluded)

Employment Class| 1982| 2004| 2010| 2016  
---|---|---|---|---  
Corporate capitalist| 0/80| 2/64| n/a| n/a  
Large Employer| 9/55| 11/37| 0/25| 11/17  
Upper Manager| 5/53| 23/33| 14/28| 17/23  
Professional Employee| 48/14| 38/10| 40/8| 41/8  
Service Worker| 41/13| 39/9| 27/13| 37/7  
Industrial Worker| 54/8| 41/11| 37/14| 49/6  
  
I would expect that American industrial and service workers and professionals
would not display as much "oppositional class consciousness" as their Canadian
counterparts, but the differences between employees, including professionals,
and managers would hold. All of this suggests that after the 1970s, when the
Ehrenreichs were writing, there is scant evidence for supposing managers and
professionals occupy a unified class that is antagonistic to wage-laborers.

Why have professionals and managers diverged over the last half-century? Our
predictions in the early 1970s that professionals were being proletarianized
seem to have been borne out. Over these decades, many professionals have
experienced a loss of autonomy and of expected income. Seventy-five years ago,
professionals--typified by the dentist, pharmacist, lawyer, and architect--
owned their own firms, and thought politically as a small business owner does.
Many were conservative Republicans. Today, many professionals work for
corporations that set their income and impose conditions on how they deliver
their services. One [_survey_](https://physiciansfoundation.org/the-
physicians-foundation-survey-finds-erosion-of-physician-autonomy-is-harming-
patient-care-driving-physician-stress-and-accelerating-workforce-
losses/?ref=compactmag.com) of doctors found that "physicians identify third-
party practice acquisition (83 percent) and rapid consolidation (74 percent)
as major contributors to autonomy loss, and more than seven in ten (75
percent) support stronger state oversight to safeguard physician leadership in
care decisions."

> "Salaried professionals find their freedom constricted."

Salaried professionals find their freedom constricted. Tech, once considered a
highly desirable career, is rapidly going down the path of deskilling. Jobs
that involve data analysis have either been automated with artificial
intelligence or shipped overseas; software engineers have become proxies for
artificial intelligence. As one
[_site_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sDy55DIkIJ0&t=239s&ref=compactmag.com)
for programmers declared: "You were never an engineer; you were a code monkey.
AI is a better code monkey than you could ever be." Many jobs that have not
been automated through AI have been outsourced thanks to remote work.

Overall white-collar salary growth has
[_stagnated_](https://www.reveliolabs.com/news/macro/white-collar-workers-are-
getting-the-blues?ref=compactmag.com) in the last two years. Much of the
reason is a weakening market for professional labor due to outsourcing,
artificial intelligence, and corporate consolidation. Between 2023 and 2025,
there was declining [_demand_](https://www.reveliolabs.com/news/macro/white-
collar-workers-are-getting-the-blues?ref=compactmag.com) for software
developers, business analysts, technology analysts, market researchers, and
data analysts, among others. But the pressure on incomes goes farther back.
Compared to 2010 and calculated in real wages, many professionals have seen
their average salaries go down. These
[_include_](https://clarifycapital.com/how-jobs-values-have-
changed?ref=compactmag.com) dentists, architects, pharmacists, economists,
engineers, nurses, writers, and actors.

Proletarianization manifests itself most dramatically in the lack of
opportunities for young people who go to college and even graduate school with
the expectation that they will gain secure, well-paying jobs as professionals.
They are the would-be professionals. According to a
[_study_](https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/college-degree-jobs-
unused-440b2abd?ref=compactmag.com) by the Burning Glass Institute, five and
ten years after obtaining their degrees, 45 percent of college graduates are
"underemployed" in jobs that don't require college degrees. Close to half of
those who obtained degrees in biology and biological sciences remain
underemployed.

Noam Scheiber recounts in his
[_book_](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250436139/mutiny/?ref=compactmag.com)
_Mutiny: The Rise and Revolt of the College-Educated Working Class_ how young
college graduates' disappointments in the labor market have radicalized many
of them. Scheiber cites a Gallup Poll finding that among the college-educated,
support for labor unions had risen to over 70 percent by the early 2020s.
Opinion analyst Nate Silver [_found_](https://www.natesilver.net/p/the-dsa-
sweet-spot-highly-educated?ref=compactmag.com) that the "most Democratic
voting group" was "voters with postgraduate degrees but lower-to-middle
household incomes of $30 thousand to $60 thousand per year." Many of these
voters, one assumes, are would-be professionals subject to proletarianization,
whose political consciousness and situation are dramatically different from
those of managers.

In a 2016 follow-up to their original essay, the Ehrenreichs themselves
acknowledged that because of the process of proletarianization, the PMC "lies
in ruins." They concluded: "The debt-ridden unemployed and underemployed
college graduates, the revenue-starved teachers, the overworked and underpaid
service professionals, even the occasional whistle-blowing scientist or
engineer--all face the same kind of situation that confronted skilled craft-
workers in the early twentieth century and all American industrial workers in
the late twentieth century."

* * *

Does this mean the diversified working class that we talked about at
_Socialist Revolution_ and in the New American Movement is now a living
reality? Would it be accurate to describe Mamdani as the candidate of the
"working class"? That would be, to say the least, a stretch. As many
professionals and would-be professionals suffer downward mobility and begin to
manifest the rudiments of a working-class consciousness, many industrial and
lower-level white collar workers in the United States have gone in the
opposite direction. There may be some convergence in economic conditions, but
not in consciousness.

That much is clear in voter preferences for the pro-union Democratic party. If
you look at Andrew Gelman's graphs, skilled and non-skilled workers became
_less_ supportive of the Democratic Party between 1976 and 2008. That trend
has continued. When Gallup asked about approval of unions in 2024, respondents
who had gone to college were 9 percentage points more approving of unions than
those with only some college and 11 points more approving than those who had
not gone to college. If you were able to translate these figures into
occupational categories, and to remove managers from the college-educated, the
disparities between salaried college-educated professionals and wage-laborers
would be even larger.

In other words, as far as shared class consciousness goes, a diversified
working class does not exist. There are many reasons for this. Differences
over cultural issues of race and sex and over socio-economic issues like
immigration have divided the potential members of a diversified working class.
These differences often intersect with differences in political geography,
[_creating_](https://johnbjudis.substack.com/p/what-are-the-democrats-chances-
this) a gulf between the world views of small town and metropolitan America.
Divisions have also arisen in between private sector industrial and white-
collar workers and the unionized public sector workers whose salaries they pay
in taxes. These divisions have contributed to the disapproval of unions among
workers who might have been expected to support them. Ruy Teixeira and I
described some of these tensions in our
[_book_](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250877499/wherehaveallthedemocratsgone/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24213367592&gbraid=0AAAAArEhehfqfBAYwDjvRrH2AylZ70SFq&gclid=Cj0KCQjwzY7VBhDwARIsAFtPvBTzlWxEtaFJ62WozsK2ffeHpVzhiMGprBuvMnnneL9cMpKlo2Y_AqAaApTSEALw_wcB&ref=compactmag.com),
_Where Have All the Democrats Gone?_

> "There are some grounds for optimism."

But there are some grounds for optimism. If you want to nourish hope that the
diversified working class we described in the early 1970s will become
conscious of itself, consider the history of the American labor movement or of
the European socialist parties. In all these cases, initial leadership did not
come from the bottom rungs, but from the top of the labor force. The American
Federation of Labor, which would eventually become the AFL-CIO, began among
craft workers suffering from proletarianization. The German Social Democratic
Party had its beginnings in the late nineteenth century among skilled artisans
and craftsmen rather than among unskilled laborers. In these cases, worsening
economic conditions and skilled political leadership eventually created common
ground, exemplified in the political transformation of the Democratic Party
during the New Deal era.

Those conditions do not currently exist in the United States. There are still
large gaps in income and status between wage-laborers and professionals, and
the political leadership that would unite them is absent. The labor movement
is weak and divided. No more than a few percent of Americans could even name
the current head of the AFL-CIO. Many Democratic Party leaders are still in
hock to culturally progressive lobbies, foundations, and think tanks. The
organization to which Mamdani and his allies belong, the Democratic Socialists
of America, purports to speak for the working class but enthusiastically
embraces the most extreme stands on immigration (open borders), crimes
(abolish the police and prisons), sex (biological men in women's sports) and
race (reparations). The PMC may be in ruins, but the diversified working
remains, at best, a work in progress.
